supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Destination Thanh Hoa Thanh Hoa police are stepping up measures to prevent and control dengue fever caused by the Dengue virus. Faced with the growing threat of dengue fever outbreaks caused by the Dengue virus, the Thanh Hoa Provincial Police are proactively implementing a comprehensive set of measures to prevent and control the epidemic; strengthening public awareness campaigns, monitoring health and environmental hygiene, promptly controlling risk factors, limiting the spread of the disease, and protecting the health of officers, soldiers, and the people. Công an tỉnh Thanh Hóa•24/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 According to statistics from October 16, 2026 to the present, Hac Thanh ward has recorded 7 cases of dengue fever with local transmission. Notably, in the outbreak area of ​​Doi Cung 2 residential group, 4 cases have appeared with signs of secondary transmission. Although epidemiological investigation, containment, and outbreak control measures have been urgently implemented, the monitoring results of the Thanh Hoa Provincial Center for Disease Control on the morning of October 23 still recorded mosquito breeding grounds and disease-transmitting mosquitoes in this area. In light of the above situation, the Director of the Provincial Police Department requested that police units and localities strengthen information and communication about the epidemic situation and preventive measures; diversify communication methods so that officers, soldiers, and citizens can proactively protect their own health, their families, and the community. When symptoms of illness appear, they should immediately go to a medical facility for examination, consultation, and timely treatment, and not self-treat at home. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA Police units and local authorities must proactively monitor the situation of outbreaks in their areas; proactively implement measures to protect the health of officers, soldiers, detainees, and drug rehabilitation trainees under the management of the Provincial Police, especially in units with large numbers of people living and eating together. Through this, they can promptly detect suspected cases, proactively coordinate handling, and prevent disease outbreaks within the units. Provincial Police spray mosquito repellent during the epidemic. You may also like Environmental sanitation and the elimination of mosquito breeding grounds are required to be carried out regularly and seriously. Units need to dispose of items and containers that can collect water and breed mosquito larvae; maintain weekly general sanitation, clear bushes, and unclog drains in the troop deployment area. Simultaneously, implement measures to eliminate mosquitoes and disease-carrying insects. The spraying of insecticides and chemicals to kill mosquitoes and insects during the autumn and winter of 2026 must be urgently implemented as required. Regarding the Hac Thanh Ward Police, the Provincial Police Director requested close coordination with the health sector to decisively and comprehensively implement disease prevention and control measures at the outbreak site in the area. This includes focusing on implementing professional measures as guided by health authorities, strengthening public awareness campaigns to encourage people to proactively clean the environment, eliminate breeding grounds for disease-carrying mosquitoes, and thoroughly address areas at risk of mosquito breeding, contributing to controlling the outbreak and limiting the risk of community spread. Regarding medical examination and treatment, the Provincial Police Hospital needs to prepare hospital beds, sufficient quantities of medicine, intravenous fluids, and treatment equipment, ensuring the "four on-site" principle; proactively receive, admit, and treat dengue fever patients, strictly implement regulations on infection control, ensure safe patient transfers, and minimize complications and deaths. Dengue fever, caused by the Dengue virus, is an acute infectious disease transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. The disease can be severe, causing dangerous complications and even death if not detected, monitored, and treated promptly. Therefore, in addition to the involvement of relevant authorities, the proactive awareness of disease prevention among each individual plays a particularly important role. You may also like To effectively prevent and control dengue fever, each family needs to regularly check and remove items that can collect water, clean water containers, and tightly cover tanks, jars, and pots; collect waste, and maintain a clean and well-ventilated living environment. People should cooperate with health forces in environmental sanitation campaigns, eliminating mosquito larvae and pupae, and spraying chemicals to kill mosquitoes; proactively prevent mosquito bites by sleeping under mosquito nets, wearing long clothing when necessary, and using appropriate mosquito repellent methods. When there are signs of suspected dengue fever, people should immediately go to a medical facility for examination, consultation, and timely treatment; under no circumstances should they attempt self-treatment at home. In particular, if warning signs appear such as severe abdominal pain, continuous vomiting, unusual bleeding, lethargy, or extreme fatigue, the patient should be taken to a medical facility immediately for prompt treatment. Every agency, unit, and family needs to proactively implement preventive measures, avoiding complacency and negligence, contributing to preventing the spread of dengue fever caused by the Dengue virus, and protecting their own health and the health of the community. supplementary_news.content_title: PAHO urges Caribbean to prepare for dengue, chikungunya rise
supplementary_news.content: PAHO urges Caribbean to prepare for dengue, chikungunya rise WASHINGTON, CMC – The Pan American Health Organisation (PAHO) is urging Caribbean countries to strengthen disease surveillance and prepare health services for possible increases in dengue and chikungunya, amid renewed transmission in parts of the Americas and the anticipated intensification of the El Niño phenomenon. In an epidemiological update issued on Wednesday, PAHO reported 1.69 million suspected dengue cases across the Americas as of mid-September, including 3,413 severe cases and 571 deaths. Although the cumulative number of reported cases was 58 per cent lower than during the same period in 2025, the agency said the decline had not been consistent across the region. It said increases had been observed in recent weeks in the Andean, Central American and Caribbean sub-regions, while all four dengue virus serotypes were circulating in the Americas in 2026. PAHO also raised concerns about chikungunya, reporting increased transmission between late 2025 and 2026, including renewed circulation in countries and territories where the virus had not been detected for several years. As of mid-September, 213,919 suspected chikungunya cases had been reported across 20 countries in the region. Of these, 78,481 were confirmed, with 88 deaths recorded. The agency also pointed to transmission in new areas, outbreaks outside historically affected seasons, longer periods of transmission and increased reports of more severe clinical manifestations. PAHO is calling for countries to strengthen epidemiological, virological and entomological surveillance, expand diagnostic capacity and ensure that cases are detected early and patients receive timely care. It also recommended stronger integrated measures to control Aedes mosquitoes, which transmit both diseases. Health services should be prepared to respond to potential increases in cases at all levels of care, PAHO said, with particular attention to strengthening primary healthcare workers’ ability to recognise dengue warning signs early and prevent progression to severe illness. Hospitals should also be ready to manage patients with warning signs and severe cases, the agency added. PAHO further urged countries to improve environmental management, remove containers that collect water and encourage communities, families, local authorities and other sectors to participate actively in mosquito prevention and control. Eliminating mosquito breeding sites remains a key measure in reducing mosquito populations, the agency said. Osprey Observer SUBMISSIONS Submit News/Press Release Bloomingdale / FishHawk Edition Current Issue Online Riverview Edition Current Issue Online Valrico Edition Current Issue Online Brandon / Winthrop Edition Current Issue Online SouthShore Edition Current Issue Online Archives 2026 Osprey Observer TV Podcasts Home Brandon / Winthrop Hillsborough County Extends Emergency Over Dengue Concerns Brandon / Winthrop County News Hillsborough County Extends Emergency Over Dengue Concerns By Marie Gilmore - October 23, 2026 108 Hillsborough County continued its response to a growing number of locally acquired dengue fever cases by extending its state of local emergency through October 22 as mosquito control crews increase efforts to reduce the mosquito population responsible for spreading the disease. County Administrator Bonnie Wise signed an executive order extending the emergency under authority granted by the county’s Emergency Management Ordinance and Chapter 252 of the Florida Statutes. The original emergency declaration was issued September 24 and has been extended in seven-day increments, including extensions through October 8, October 15 and October 22. A state of local emergency may remain in effect for seven days unless it is rescinded or extended. The declaration allows county officials and emergency managers to take certain actions more quickly to protect the health, safety and welfare of residents. It also provides a path for reimbursement of certain emergency-related expenses. Mosquito Management crews are increasing treatments by both air and ground after surveillance identified dengue virus activity in mosquito populations in multiple neighborhoods. The county is coordinating with the Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County on education and mosquito-control efforts in impacted areas. Hillsborough County has reported more than 200 locally acquired dengue cases during the outbreak, making up the vast majority of Florida’s reported cases. The outbreak has affected communities across the county, with cases identified in nearly 60 ZIP codes. Dengue is spread primarily by infected Aedes mosquitoes. Symptoms can include a sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle, bone or joint pain, nausea, vomiting and a rash. Most people recover within two to seven days. Residents should seek emergency medical care if warning signs of severe dengue develop, including severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, extreme fatigue or irritability or difficulty breathing. Residents throughout the county are encouraged to help reduce mosquito breeding areas by eliminating standing water around their homes, particularly following recent heavy rains. Residents can also sign up for notifications about localized aerial treatments in their neighborhoods and access information about current mosquito-control activities through the county’s online resources. Mosquito control services are funded in part through Hillsborough County property tax dollars. For more information, contact Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services at 813-635-5400

supplementary_news.content: ___ Play Now Log InSign Up Florida News Listen Live National News Weird News Local Traffic Local Weather Get News Alerts Florida News Florida Dengue Cases Top 400 as Mosquito-Borne Virus Spreads By Rob Garguilo Oct 23, 2026 Photo: Brett_Hondow / iStock / Getty Images FLORIDA - Florida health officials are reporting additional locally acquired dengue fever infections as the mosquito-borne virus spreads into more counties across the state. The Florida Department of Health reports that locally transmitted dengue cases have surpassed 400 in 2026, with the Tampa Bay region accounting for most infections. Hillsborough County remains the center of the outbreak, while neighboring Pinellas and Pasco counties continue reporting additional cases. According to Pinellas County officials, 401 dengue cases have been confirmed across the three counties, representing a 14% increase from the previous week. Pinellas County has recorded 51 confirmed cases since August and extended its local state of emergency through October 29th. The declaration allows county officials to accelerate mosquito control operations and seek potential reimbursement for related expenses. Locally acquired infections have also been identified in Miami-Dade, Broward, Orange, Palm Beach and Polk counties. Seminole County recently confirmed its first locally transmitted case. Mosquito control agencies are expanding surveillance, conducting ground spraying and coordinating aerial treatments to reduce mosquito populations. Planned helicopter treatments in Pinellas County have been delayed because of high winds, with operations expected to begin next week if weather conditions permit. Dengue spreads through infected mosquito bites and can cause fever, headaches, muscle pain, joint pain, nausea and skin rashes. Severe infections may require hospitalization. Health officials recommend eliminating standing water, wearing protective clothing and applying EPA-registered insect repellents to prevent mosquito bites. supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế A 23-year-old man with critical dengue fever requires ECMO intervention. GĐXH - After 5 days of high fever, abdominal pain, and digestive disorders, the young man went into shock and suffered critical respiratory failure. Doctors had to deploy ECMO combined with continuous hemodialysis to support the patient's vital functions. Báo Gia đình và Xã hội•26/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Dengue fever can become severe even in young people with no underlying health conditions. On October 26th, information from the Central Hospital for Tropical Diseases indicated that doctors there are treating 18 dengue fever patients, including one critical case requiring ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation) intervention. According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, patient LTS (23 years old, residing in Tuyen Quang ) had no prior recorded underlying medical conditions. The patient developed a high fever and abdominal pain, and self-medicated at home, but their condition did not improve. By the third day, the patient also experienced frequent loose stools, nausea, and fatigue. A critically ill dengue fever patient is being treated at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Photo: Provided by the hospital. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA The patient was taken to a nearby medical facility, diagnosed with dengue fever, and treated with intravenous fluids. However, the patient's condition continued to worsen, with significant fatigue, agitation, hypotension, and respiratory failure. The patient required intubation and mechanical ventilation before being transferred to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Upon admission, the patient was in critical condition. Despite invasive mechanical ventilation with 100% oxygen, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) was only about 80%. Heart rate was rapid at 120-140 beats/minute, blood pressure was 80/40 mmHg despite the use of vasopressors. The patient was cyanotic, had cold extremities, and bilateral pulmonary hypoventilation. Laboratory results showed positive NS1 and IgM Dengue tests, along with abnormalities in liver, kidney, and coagulation functions. Doctors diagnosed the patient with dengue hemorrhagic shock, critical respiratory failure progressing to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and suspected gastrointestinal infection. According to Dr. Phuc, this is a particularly severe case of dengue fever in a young person with no underlying medical conditions. The shock and severe lung damage directly threaten the patient's life. You may also like Implement ECMO in combination with continuous renal replacement therapy to support life. Faced with severe respiratory failure and no improvement in blood oxygen levels despite mechanical ventilation at maximum oxygen concentration, doctors at the Intensive Care Unit decided to implement extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) to support gas exchange. In addition to ECMO, the patient was treated with mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, and continuous hemodialysis. A combination of resuscitation measures was employed to support circulation, manage metabolic disorders, balance fluids, and support renal function according to the patient's clinical condition. During treatment, patients are closely monitored for hemodynamic parameters, coagulation, and organ function to allow for timely adjustments to resuscitation measures. Following intensive resuscitation, the patient's blood oxygenation and hemodynamic status initially improved. The oxygen concentration delivered via ventilator was reduced to 21%, and blood pressure was recorded at approximately 100/70 mmHg while the patient was still receiving vasopressors. However, the patient still requires VV-ECMO support and intensive care measures. The patient has not yet been assessed as having passed the critical stage and needs continued close monitoring and treatment. Be vigilant for dengue fever during the period from day 3 to day 7. According to Dr. Phuc, dengue fever is an infectious disease caused by the dengue virus, primarily transmitted through Aedes mosquitoes. The disease can affect people of all ages, including young, healthy individuals without underlying health conditions. Most people with dengue fever recover, but some cases can become severe due to plasma leakage, leading to shock, severe bleeding, and organ damage. It's important to note that the critical phase usually occurs from the 3rd to the 7th day of the illness, especially when the patient's fever begins to subside or has just disappeared. This is when plasma leakage, blood concentration, thrombocytopenia, and shock can occur. Therefore, the absence of fever does not mean the patient is cured. You may also like Based on the above case, Dr. Phuc advises people not to be complacent when experiencing prolonged high fever, especially when warning signs appear such as severe or continuous abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, extreme fatigue, restlessness, lethargy, unusual bleeding, decreased urination, or difficulty breathing. When these symptoms appear, patients should immediately go to a medical facility for timely assessment and treatment. Those suspected of having dengue fever should not self-administer intravenous fluids at home or use aspirin, ibuprofen, and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) due to the risk of increased bleeding. Fluid replacement, fever reduction medication, and laboratory monitoring should be carried out according to the instructions of healthcare professionals. Besides early detection and treatment, people need to proactively prevent the disease by eliminating mosquito breeding grounds, covering water containers, destroying mosquito larvae, and avoiding mosquito bites. People can also learn about dengue fever vaccination according to age, indications, and professional guidance from doctors. supplementary_news.content: Latest Bangladesh Business World Sports Opinion Politics Diplomacy More E-Paper ☀️ 🌐 English বাংলা Russian Hindi Chinese Trending Saudi-Houthi Conflict Tarique Rahman Israel Election Road Accident Mirpur Test × Today's Newspaper Latest World Cup Magazine 2026 Election 2026 Follow Us Print: 29 Oct 2026 Bangladesh Dengue spreads to villages as death toll hits 377 Experts want entomologist-led, scientifically tested mosquito control Hedayet Ullah Khan Published: 25 Oct 2026, 12:00 AM Updated: 25 Oct 2026, 11:07 AM Share Share options Print Copy link Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin A A Dengue has killed 377 people across the country this year, 132 of them in the first 24 days of October, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), as public health experts say the disease is spreading from cities into districts and rural communities where local authorities lack the capacity to control mosquitoes. Six people died in the 24 hours to 8am on Saturday, while 1,898 patients were admitted to hospitals during the period. Cumulative admissions since 1 January have reached 1,21,699. Two of the latest victims were from Chattogram division, and one each from Dhaka South City Corporation, Khulna division, Mymensingh and Rajshahi division. Dengue claimed 43 lives in August and 148 in September, the highest monthly figure this year, before October’s 132 deaths. Dhaka division, including the two city corporations, has recorded 180 deaths, followed by Khulna (67), Chattogram (37), Mymensingh (31), Barishal (28), Rajshahi (24), Rangpur (7) and Sylhet (3). The DGHS recorded 413 dengue deaths in 2025. Public health experts say the disease is no longer confined to Dhaka and other cities. Prof Dr Be-Nazir Ahmed, public health strategist and former director of Disease Control at Directorate General of Health Services, told the Daily Sun that dengue, once regarded as primarily urban, is becoming established in rural areas. He cited the presence of aedes mosquitoes there and widespread domestic travel, which carries the virus to new areas as infected people move around the country. “Dengue will remain a risk for Bangladesh in the coming days. I believe it will pose an even greater challenge. In particular, it could become a devastating disease in rural areas,” he said. He said union parishads struggle to carry out effective mosquito-control operations, while many municipalities lack the necessary manpower, equipment and institutional capacity. Read More Measles, dengue claim 10 more lives in 24hrs Prevention measures must be set up at union, upazila and municipal levels as well as in major cities, he said, or rising rural infections could become increasingly difficult to manage. Dr Mushtuq Husain, public health expert and advisor to Institute of Epidemiology Disease Control and Research, said dengue has been a major challenge since 2020, with a severe outbreak in 2023. It has now reached remote districts such as Barguna and Satkhira, he said, with human movement carrying the virus to areas where aedes mosquitoes allow local transmission. Be-Nazir Ahmed said aedes mosquitoes generally breed in stagnant clean water around homes, including on rooftops and balconies and in flowerpots, water containers, construction sites and abandoned properties. Water collecting in potholes and open spaces, and poor waste management, also create favourable conditions. Spraying insecticide alone cannot control dengue without addressing these causes, he said, adding that authorities need to identify breeding sites and high-infection areas and base strategies on reliable data. In many areas, mosquito-control drives are held but stagnant water is not regularly removed, he noted. Dr Mushtuq urged authorities to involve entomologists in mosquito-control programmes, saying decisions on which insecticides to use, and how and where to apply them, should rest on scientific assessment. Control workers need proper training, he said, and insecticides should be tested regularly. Authorities must also evaluate whether operations are reducing mosquito populations and transmission, rather than focusing on visible campaigns and publicity. Criticising the government’s approach, he said, “If you tie a horse to a post and whip it, it will run with all its might, but it will not move an inch forward. The government’s approach is much the same.” DGHS age-specific data show that 17,409 patients this year were aged 21 to 25, the highest among the five-year age groups. Another 17,200 were aged 26 to 30 and 16,446 were aged 16 to 20. More than 6,200 children under five were also affected. Dr Mushtuq said young people may be more exposed to aedes mosquitoes because they spend more time outside the home for work and education. Be-Nazir Ahmed pointed to prior infections. There are four main dengue serotypes, and infection with one does not necessarily protect against the others. A later infection with a different serotype can increase the risk of severe dengue in some cases. Older people may have developed immunity to all four through earlier infections, unlike younger people, he said. Read More Cox’s Bazar tourism boom exposes gaps in visitor safety Most patients recover with appropriate care, but some develop complications, including plasma leakage, low blood pressure, severe bleeding and impaired organ function. Health experts said the period when fever subsides is particularly critical, as severe symptoms can develop within 24 to 48 hours. Warning signs include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, unusual weakness, restlessness, breathing difficulties, cold hands and feet, and reduced urine output. Anyone with these symptoms should seek urgent medical attention. Many patients initially mistake dengue for ordinary fever and delay seeking care. Treatment requires fluid management based on the patient’s condition, monitoring of blood pressure and urine output, and necessary tests. Patients should not take excessive fluids or intravenous saline on their own, experts said. Paracetamol may be used for fever under medical guidance, but aspirin, ibuprofen and certain other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can increase the risk of bleeding and should be avoided unless a qualified physician advises otherwise. Experts said adding beds is not enough. Hospitals must also be able to identify patients whose condition is deteriorating rapidly, through complete blood count tests, haematocrit monitoring, assessment of fluid intake and urine output, and intensive care for severe cases. Not every patient needs admission, they said, as the decision should rest on symptoms and a physician’s assessment, though patients with warning signs need prompt attention. They also called for coordination between public and private hospitals, adequate staffing, access to diagnostic tests, stronger emergency capacity and regularly updated infection and mortality data. Seasonal campaigns alone cannot control dengue, the experts said, calling for year-round efforts to eliminate breeding sites, strengthen surveillance, improve waste management and raise public awareness, even when cases are low. Unless local capacity is strengthened from cities to villages, mosquito control becomes more scientific and patients receive timely treatment, dengue is likely to remain a major public health threat in Bangladesh, they said. (WWSB) - Health officials have confirmed a human case of locally acquired dengue in Manatee County. The Florida Department of Health in Manatee County said it is working with Manatee County Mosquito Control to increase surveillance and prevention efforts. Those efforts include removing mosquito breeding areas and aerial spraying. The confirmation marks a change from earlier this month, when local officials said there were no confirmed locally acquired dengue cases in Manatee County. Local mosquito authorities kicking up protocol midst Dengue Fever surge Health officials are urging residents to take steps to avoid mosquito bites. The Department of Health said it continues statewide monitoring for mosquito-borne illnesses, including dengue, West Nile virus, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, malaria and chikungunya. The advisory did not identify where in Manatee County the person may have been exposed. It also did not provide the patient’s condition, the number of locally acquired cases or details about planned aerial-spraying areas and dates. Residents can report dead birds to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, according to the department. Copyright 2026 WWSB. All rights reserved. We are grateful that the land can finally be wet again and the forest fires can be extinguished immediately. However, this season change also brings health challenges that should not be ignored, one of which is the increased risk of dengue fever (DBD). Sejarah Indonesia Temukan lebih banyak Baca Isu Politik Pemerintah Cek Layanan This disease transmitted by the bite of the Aedes aegypti mosquito can attack anyone, from children to adults. Therefore, we need to know the causes of the increase in dengue fever cases during the rainy season and what can be done as a preventive measure. The following is a discussion. Why Does Dengue Fever Risk Increase During Rainy Season? There are several factors that increase the risk of dengue fever during the rainy season. Reported from Continental Hospitals, here are some things you need to know. Many Water Stains The main reason why dengue fever spreads faster during the rainy season is none other than the many puddles. We can find puddles in various places, ranging from plant pots, old tires, to clogged water drains. Water that is contained in these places can become a location for Aedes aegypti mosquitoes to lay eggs if the conditions are right. "We must remember, these mosquitoes do not breed in dirty ponds or waterways. They actually need relatively clean water puddles to lay eggs. Mosquito Development is Supported by Environmental Conditions Warm temperatures combined with high humidity during the rainy season support the development of mosquitoes from eggs to adults. When breeding sites are available in large numbers, mosquito populations have the potential to increase in a relatively short time. Mosquito Activity in the Daytime This increased humidity also makes Aedes aegypti mosquitoes more active. This type of mosquito is different from other mosquitoes that generally bite at night. This dengue-carrying mosquito is more active during the day, especially in the morning and afternoon. Therefore, even if you are at home or at work, you are still at risk of being bitten by Aedes mosquitoes. How to Prevent Dengue Fever at Home During Rainy Season Preventing dengue fever is not enough just by maintaining the cleanliness of the house and yard when the rainy season comes. Reported from the same page, here are some steps that can be taken inside and outside the house to prevent dengue transmission. Make Sure There Is No Water Stains Check the home environment at least once a week to ensure there are no containers that can potentially hold water. If there are, empty, brush, cover, or remove the items so that they do not become a place for mosquitoes to lay eggs. Temukan lebih banyak Pemerintahan Cari Peta Wilayah Tur Asia Tenggara You need to pay attention to the containers used daily, such as pet drinking places, water coolers, or plant pot holders. Clean the container regularly and make sure there are no puddles. Use Anti Mosquito Lotion You can use lotion or mosquito repellent products to help reduce the risk of bites while at home and outdoors. Choose products with active ingredients that have been approved by the Ministry of Health and use them according to the instructions on the packaging. Wear Clothes that Cover the Skin When you are outside the house, wear long-sleeved clothes and long pants. You can also use socks and shoes to help reduce the skin that is open to mosquito bites. Although it does not completely eliminate the risk of bites, clothing that covers the skin can be an additional protection. Use Mosquito Net While Sleeping Mosquito nets can help protect family members from mosquito bites while sleeping, including during naps. The use of mosquito nets while sleeping is especially for babies, small children, and the elderly who need more protection during rest. Make sure the mosquito net is properly attached and does not leave gaps that allow mosquitoes to enter. That is a discussion of a number of things you need to know about the increased risk of dengue fever during the rainy season and the prevention measures. By implementing the prevention measures above, you also help reduce the risk of transmission of DBD in the community. If you experience dengue fever symptoms, immediately contact a doctor so that you can get the right treatment immediately. The information is then handed over to the state for its eradication efforts. By Kevin Killough Published: October 26, 2026 7:48am Article Dig Deeper Benjamin Jacob, University of South Florida professor, and a team of researchers, are using artificial intelligence to target breeding grounds for mosquitoes carrying the dengue virus in an effort to address an outbreak of dengue fever in Florida. Cases of the disease have spiked this year, where 425 locally acquired cases have been reported. There were an additional 288 international cases reported as well. The outbreak was largely concentrated in Hillsborough County, which surrounds Tampa, The Hill reported. Jacob's system uses satellite images along with weather patterns and known breeding grounds to identify potential locations quickly. The information is then handed over to the state for its eradication efforts. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 28, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Autoimmune disease linked to greater dengue severity in Colombian cohort by October 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Autoimmune disease linked to greater dengue severity in Colombian cohort Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram The study included 171 participants whose outcomes were assessed over 2014–2024: 57 had autoimmune diseases and 114 did not. Severe dengue occurred in 7.0% of the autoimmune-disease group, compared with 2.6% of the comparison group. After adjustment for potential confounders, the association between autoimmune disease and dengue severity was estimated at an odds ratio of 2.14, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.08–4.41 and p = 0.030. The researchers compared demographic, clinical and outcome measures between the two groups and examined laboratory-test trends before, during and after infection. Women represented 87.7% of the sample, and the median age was 48 years. Among participants with autoimmune diseases, rheumatoid arthritis was the most frequent diagnosis at 42%, followed by systemic lupus erythematosus at 29.8% and Sjögren’s syndrome at 19.3%. Patients with autoimmune diseases more often presented with dengue warning signs: these were reported in 66.7% of the autoimmune-disease group and 55.4% of the group without autoimmune diseases. The study also found a higher proportion reporting a previous dengue infection in the autoimmune-disease group, at 49.1% compared with 43.0%. Hospitalization was more frequent among participants with autoimmune disease, at 68.4% versus 61.4%, but that difference was not statistically significant, with p = 0.368. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Treatments Explore Data infection Intensive-care admission was also numerically higher in the autoimmune-disease group, at 12.3% versus 5.3%, although the difference did not reach statistical significance, with p = 0.125. Participants with autoimmune diseases had longer hospital stays, but the supplied research summary does not report the numerical durations. For the severity analysis, the investigators calculated crude and adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals to identify factors associated with dengue severity. They also performed sensitivity analyses, interaction testing and bootstrap validation, and reported that the findings were consistent across the adjusted, sensitivity and bootstrap analyses. The authors described this consistency as support for the robustness of the association within the dataset. Dengue is an acute viral illness transmitted by the mosquitoes Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus and is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Although most infections are asymptomatic, severe disease can develop, particularly in people with risk factors. The researchers noted that the clinical course of dengue had been studied less extensively in patients with autoimmune diseases and that no prior research on this question had been conducted in Colombia. Larger prospective multicenter studies were needed to confirm the association and clarify its immunopathogenic basis. supplementary_news.content: Pasar al contenido principal Main navigation Inicio Áreas y temas Temas prioritarios Grupos estables investigación Ciencias exactas y tecnología Economía, Negocios y Desarrollo Humanidades, artes y disciplinas creativas Persona y Sociedad Salud Integral y Bienestar Investigadores Publicaciones Libros en coedición Libros de acceso abierto Revistas académicas Eventos Encuentro de investigadores Encuentro de la RIU Concurso de Carteles FIL Guadalajara Simposio Institucional Contacto Buscar Evaluation of dengue virus seroprevalence in four boroughs of Mexico City among persons aged 5-35 years in 2022 Autor/es Anáhuac Coba-Alcalá Eleazar; González-Roldán Jesús Felipe; Ramos-Castañeda José Año de publicación 2025 Journal o Editorial Journal of Infection in Developing Countries Abstract Introduction: Dengue is currently the most widespread vector-borne disease, and its transmission has been intensively studied in endemic/hyperendemic localities. However, to obtain a complete picture of dengue transmission, it is necessary to study nonendemic localities. Imported dengue cases have been reported in Mexico City, and the presence of eggs of the vector Aedes aegyptihas been detected. Methodology: In the present study, we determined the prevalence of IgG antibodies against Dengue virus in four city boroughs via random cluster sampling in individuals aged 5-35 years. Results: The weighted seroprevalence rate was 1.90% (95% CI 0.75-4.75) at Xochimilco, 1.81% (95% CI 0.64-5.00) at Venustiano Carranza, 1.81% (95% CI 0.54-5.83) at Tlahuac, and 5.48% (95% CI 1.96-14.43) at Gustavo A Madero; seropositivity was concentrated in the adult group, many of whom lived in dengue-endemic localities. The distribution of seroprevalence in the four boroughs is very homogeneous and unrelated to the number of vector eggs in the borough. Conclusions: These data suggest that there is still no autochthonous transmission of dengue in Mexico City. However, it is important to note that the structural conditions of the dwellings in these boroughs, which offer minimal barriers to vector infestation, could facilitate the establishment of local transmission under favorable conditions. supplementary_news.content_title: Human challenge study reveals how preexisting immunity affects dengue
supplementary_news.content: Dengue virus is especially pernicious compared with many other viruses, as secondary infections can actually be worse than the first one. Now, a new phase 1 trial involving controlled infections in volunteers provides a treasure trove of details about how preexisting immunity and anti-dengue antibodies affect the nature of secondary infections with dengue. The findings are among the first to glean insights using a large controlled human challenge, and could inform future therapeutics and the design of more broadly protective vaccines. Secondary infections with dengue are often the most severe ones, as preexisting antibodies can boost viral counts and raise the risk of severe symptoms. This has frustrated the development of badly needed vaccines for dengue. Furthermore, it's been challenging to understand how pre-infection affects dengue outcomes, as animal models have many limitations and patients usually don't present until after viral counts have peaked. In this study, Camila Odio and colleagues recruited 45 healthy adults who had either zero, one, or more than one prior infection with any of the four strains of dengue virus (DENV1-DENV4). The volunteers received injections of a live, weakened strain of DENV3 in a challenge study, allowing the researchers to fully interrogate dengue immunity dynamics in humans in a safe and controlled setting. The team made various discoveries: for example, they found that people whose antibodies boosted the replication of the virus had the highest viral counts and waning of CD8-bearing T cells and antibodies. Meanwhile, people who had higher amounts of antibodies against the viral nonstructural protein 1 displayed more balanced immune responses and lower viral counts. "Collectively, this work confirms multiple hypotheses generated by natural history studies and reveals the optimal conditions for inducing potent and persistent immunity against DENV1 to DENV4," Odio et al. conclude. Source: Journal reference: Odio, C. D., et al . (2026). Dengue virus controlled human challenge reveals that preexisting immunity shapes viral replication and broadly protective responses. Science Translational Medicine. DOI: 10.1126/scitranslmed.aei5117. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/scitranslmed.aei5117

supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế A 23-year-old with no underlying conditions went into dengue shock and required 13 days of intensive care before ECMO was removed. Despite having no underlying medical conditions, the young man still went into dengue hemorrhagic shock, suffering severe lung damage that required ECMO and dialysis to maintain his vital functions. Báo Khoa học và Đời sống•26/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 SpO2 dropped to 80%, causing shock and critical respiratory failure despite the patient being young and having no underlying medical conditions. According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, patient LTS (23 years old, residing in Tuyen Quang ) had no prior recorded underlying medical conditions. The patient developed a high fever and abdominal pain, and self-medicated at home without improvement. On the third day, the patient experienced frequent loose stools, nausea, and fatigue. After being taken to a nearby medical facility, the patient was diagnosed with dengue fever and treated with intravenous fluids. However, the condition continued to worsen with symptoms of extreme fatigue, agitation, hypotension, and respiratory failure. The patient required intubation and mechanical ventilation before being transferred to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Patients receiving care at the hospital - Photo courtesy of the hospital. Upon admission, the patient was in critical condition. Despite invasive mechanical ventilation with 100% oxygen, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) was only about 80%. Heart rate was rapid at 120–140 beats/minute, blood pressure was 80/40 mmHg despite the use of vasopressors. The patient was cyanotic, had cold extremities, and bilateral pulmonary hypoventilation. Test results showed a positive Dengue test, along with abnormal liver, kidney, and coagulation function. The patient was diagnosed with Dengue hemorrhagic shock, critical respiratory failure progressing to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and suspected gastrointestinal infection. According to Dr. Phuc, this is a particularly severe case of dengue fever in a young person with no underlying health conditions, presenting with shock and severe lung damage, directly threatening their life. Given the patient's oxygen saturation did not improve despite mechanical ventilation at maximum oxygen concentration, the doctors decided to implement extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) to support gas exchange. Simultaneously, the patient received vasopressors, continuous hemodialysis, and resuscitation measures to support circulation, control metabolic disorders, balance fluids, and support kidney function. The patient is being kept alive using ECMO - Photo courtesy of the hospital. After 13 days of intensive care, the patient was weaned off ECMO. By 3 PM on October 26th, after 13 days of intensive treatment at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, patient LTS's condition had improved significantly. The patient had been weaned off ECMO and the endotracheal tube, is now conscious, and continues to be monitored and cared for at the hospital. You may also like The patient is expected to be discharged on October 27th if their health remains stable and they meet the discharge criteria. From a state of dengue hemorrhagic shock and critical respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation with maximum oxygen concentration, the patient gradually recovered after a prolonged intensive resuscitation process. This case demonstrates that dengue fever can be severe even in young people without underlying medical conditions. Early detection of warning signs and timely access to treatment are crucial in limiting the risk of serious complications. The fever subsiding does not mean the dangerous phase is over. According to Dr. Phuc, dengue fever is an infectious disease caused by the dengue virus, primarily transmitted through Aedes mosquitoes. The disease can affect people of all ages. Most people recover, but some cases can become severe due to plasma leakage, leading to shock, severe bleeding, and organ damage. The critical phase usually occurs from the 3rd to the 7th day of the illness, especially when the patient's fever begins to subside or has just disappeared. This is when plasma leakage, blood concentration, thrombocytopenia, and shock can occur. Therefore, patients should not be complacent when they see their body temperature drop. Doctors examine patients after the critical stage - Photo courtesy of the hospital. Dr. Phuc advises people to seek medical attention immediately if they experience warning signs such as severe or persistent abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, extreme fatigue, restlessness, lethargy, unusual bleeding, decreased urination, or difficulty breathing. Individuals suspected of having dengue fever should not self-administer intravenous fluids at home or use aspirin, ibuprofen, and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) due to the risk of increased bleeding. Fluid replacement, fever reduction medication, and laboratory monitoring should be administered according to the instructions of healthcare professionals. Currently, the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases is treating 18 dengue fever patients. Besides early detection of worsening symptoms, people need to proactively eliminate mosquito breeding grounds, cover water containers tightly, kill mosquito larvae, and prevent mosquito bites. Understanding dengue fever vaccination should also be based on age, indications, and current professional guidelines. Symptoms of dengue fever that require immediate medical attention. - Severe or persistent abdominal pain. You may also like - Frequent vomiting, extreme fatigue. - Struggling, sluggish. - Abnormal bleeding. - Infrequent urination or difficulty breathing. Submit a News Tip Contests Sports In Between The Lines Friday Night Game Night Game of the Week Athlete of the Week Nominate an Athlete A-List Talks Podcast Suncoast View Hot Topics Suncoast Stories Suncoast Kitchens Sponsored Segments Videos Full Episodes NowCast Community Animal Outtakes Community Calendar Chalkboard Champions Day of Giving Empowering Voices Health Experts Help the Hungry Heroes Among Us Lottery Numbers Money Matters New Businesses Osprey Cams Pet of the Week Saluting the Suncoast Sponsored Stories Suncoast View This Day In History We the People Entertainment Aging Untold Weather Forecast Hurricane LiveCams Fish & Game Forecast About Us ABC7 Digital Media Advertise With Us Careers Meet the Team Contact Us Programming Schedule Download Our Apps PowerNation NextGen TV Circle Country Local News Live InvestigateTV Watching Your Wallet Digital Marketing Gray AI Policy Dengue fever case confirmed in Manatee County as cases rise across Florida Close WWSB ABC7 News at 6pm By Juliana Narvaez Published: Oct. 23, 2026 at 11:08 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google MANATEE COUNTY, Fla. (WWSB) - A mosquito-borne illness typically associated with tropical regions is reaching new highs in Florida. And now, there’s one confirmed case in Manatee County. According to the Florida Department of Health’s latest data, more than 400 cases of locally acquired dengue fever have been reported across the state this year. Dengue is a viral infection spread to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito. Christopher Lesser, director of the Manatee County Mosquito Control District, says the district has been taking preventative measures in areas where the disease is more likely to occur. “We’ve been treating our urban areas where this disease normally occurs, once every two weeks. This would be all of Palmetto, all of Bradenton, as a preventative measure,” Lesser said. Lesser says the district has been working to keep mosquito populations low amid a broader dengue outbreak across the Tampa Bay area. He says the mosquito population in urban areas has remained particularly low over the past several months. The mosquito species most commonly associated with spreading dengue, Aedes aegypti, is not common in Manatee County. However, Lesser says residents should remain cautious about mosquito-borne illnesses and mosquito bites in general. So far, there have been no reported cases of locally acquired dengue fever in Sarasota County. Jackie Lebouitz, a chemical in the environment agent with UF/IFAS Extension Sarasota County, says residents should know what symptoms to watch for. Many people who contract dengue do not develop symptoms. For those who do, symptoms can include headaches, fatigue, muscle soreness and, sometimes, a rash. Lebouitz says there are also simple steps people can take to reduce their risk of being bitten. She recommends wearing light-colored, loose-fitting clothing, including long sleeves and pants. She also advises using an EPA-registered insect repellent on exposed skin. While local mosquito control officials continue working to keep mosquito populations down, experts say personal prevention remains an important part of reducing the risk of infection. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 28, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Autoimmune disease linked to greater dengue severity in Colombian cohort by October 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Autoimmune disease linked to greater dengue severity in Colombian cohort Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram The study included 171 participants whose outcomes were assessed over 2014–2024: 57 had autoimmune diseases and 114 did not. Severe dengue occurred in 7.0% of the autoimmune-disease group, compared with 2.6% of the comparison group. After adjustment for potential confounders, the association between autoimmune disease and dengue severity was estimated at an odds ratio of 2.14, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.08–4.41 and p = 0.030. The researchers compared demographic, clinical and outcome measures between the two groups and examined laboratory-test trends before, during and after infection. Women represented 87.7% of the sample, and the median age was 48 years. Among participants with autoimmune diseases, rheumatoid arthritis was the most frequent diagnosis at 42%, followed by systemic lupus erythematosus at 29.8% and Sjögren’s syndrome at 19.3%. Patients with autoimmune diseases more often presented with dengue warning signs: these were reported in 66.7% of the autoimmune-disease group and 55.4% of the group without autoimmune diseases. The study also found a higher proportion reporting a previous dengue infection in the autoimmune-disease group, at 49.1% compared with 43.0%. Hospitalization was more frequent among participants with autoimmune disease, at 68.4% versus 61.4%, but that difference was not statistically significant, with p = 0.368. Intensive-care admission was also numerically higher in the autoimmune-disease group, at 12.3% versus 5.3%, although the difference did not reach statistical significance, with p = 0.125. Participants with autoimmune diseases had longer hospital stays, but the supplied research summary does not report the numerical durations. For the severity analysis, the investigators calculated crude and adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals to identify factors associated with dengue severity. They also performed sensitivity analyses, interaction testing and bootstrap validation, and reported that the findings were consistent across the adjusted, sensitivity and bootstrap analyses. The authors described this consistency as support for the robustness of the association within the dataset. Dengue is an acute viral illness transmitted by the mosquitoes Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus and is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Although most infections are asymptomatic, severe disease can develop, particularly in people with risk factors. The researchers noted that the clinical course of dengue had been studied less extensively in patients with autoimmune diseases and that no prior research on this question had been conducted in Colombia. Larger prospective multicenter studies were needed to confirm the association and clarify its immunopathogenic basis. After five days of high fever, abdominal pain, and digestive disorders, the 23-year-old man went into shock and suffered critical respiratory failure. VietNamNet • 26/10/2026 On October 26th, the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases ( Hanoi ) reported that it is currently treating 18 dengue fever patients. Notably, patient LTS (23 years old, residing in Tuyen Quang), who had no prior medical conditions, is in critical condition. Mr. S. developed a high fever and abdominal pain, and self-medicated at home without improvement. On the third day, he experienced frequent loose stools, nausea, and fatigue. After being taken to a nearby medical facility, he was diagnosed with dengue fever and treated with intravenous fluids. However, his condition continued to worsen, developing agitation, hypotension, and respiratory failure, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation before being transferred to a higher-level facility. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA Upon admission to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, Mr. S. was in critical condition, his entire body was cyanotic, his extremities were cold, and he had reduced ventilation in both lungs. The patient was admitted to the emergency room in critical condition. Photo: Provided by the hospital. (Baohatinh.vn) - The People's Committee of Ha Tinh province has just approved the Project on rearranging and reorganizing units under the Department of Health in the direction of streamlining the organizational structure, effectively utilizing resources, and improving the quality of medical examination and treatment. Is it better to measure blood pressure in the morning or at night? What does a doctor advise? In healthy adults, blood pressure typically drops to its lowest level during deep sleep. Afterward, blood pressure begins to gradually rise about 1-2 hours before waking and is usually higher in the morning. Stroke doesn't discriminate by age: Silent risks people under 45 should be aware of. Stroke is often considered a disease of older adults, but in reality, young people can also experience this event. The cause may be related to risk factors that have silently accumulated over many years. Tests confirmed a positive Dengue test, along with abnormal liver, kidney, and coagulation function. The patient was diagnosed with Dengue hemorrhagic shock, critical respiratory failure progressing to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Given that the patient's blood oxygen levels did not improve despite mechanical ventilation at maximum oxygen concentration, The doctors decided to implement extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) to support respiration. The patient was also given vasopressors, continuous hemodialysis, and close monitoring of organ function. According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, this was a particularly severe case of dengue fever in a young person with no underlying conditions. The shock and severe lung damage directly threatened the patient's life, requiring a combination of intensive resuscitation measures. You may also like By 3 PM on October 26th, after 13 days of intensive treatment, patient S.'s condition had improved. The patient was weaned off ECMO and the endotracheal tube was removed. The patient is now conscious and continues to be monitored and cared for at the hospital. Based on this case, Dr. Phuc warned that dengue fever can become severe even in young, healthy individuals without underlying conditions. The disease is primarily transmitted through Aedes mosquitoes. In some cases, plasma leakage may occur, leading to shock, severe bleeding, and organ damage. supplementary_news.content: Skip to content Wednesday, October 28, 2026 About Us Contact X-twitter Instagram Facebook Home News Eats Sports Lifestyle Real Estate Home News Eats Sports Lifestyle Real Estate 0 Search Home Health » News Dengue cases rise in Florida: What to know about symptoms By Selim Algar on October 23, 2026 on 2:47 pm Updated on: 10/23/2026 Share this post : Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Dr. Hongfei Di of Paradigm Primary Care. Florida added 57 locally acquired dengue cases to its latest weekly tally, and a St. Johns County doctor says recognizing symptoms can help patients know when to get checked. The state has recorded 425 cases acquired in Florida this year, according to the Department of Health’s report for Oct. 11–17. Dr. Hongfei Di, of Paradigm Primary Care and Wellness, said the early symptoms can be misleading. “Dengue fever sounds bad, but the initial presentation is just like your common cold or flu,” Dr. Di said. St. Johns County has recorded three travel-associated dengue cases this year, meaning those people were infected elsewhere. No locally acquired cases have been reported in the county thus far, according to the state report. Most cases have been reported in Hillsborough and Pinellas counties. About one in four people infected with dengue develop symptoms, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Those can include fever, headaches, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint aches, nausea and a rash. Most people who become ill recover after about a week. Dr. Hongfei Di at his Nocatee office. Patients should tell their healthcare provider about recent travel and mosquito exposure, which can help guide evaluation. “When you really do need to seek help is if you have any signs of gum bleeding, nosebleeds, or easily bruising all of a sudden,” Dr. Di said. About one in 20 people who become sick develop severe dengue, according to the CDC. Warning signs include abdominal pain, repeated vomiting and extreme tiredness or restlessness. Those signs commonly appear within 24 to 48 hours after the fever goes away, when patients may think they are recovering. There is no specific medicine to treat dengue. For mild illness, care generally involves rest, fluids and acetaminophen for fever or pain. Using mosquito repellent and emptying standing water around the home can help prevent bites. Paradigm Primary Care and Wellness is an advertising partner of St. Johns Citizen. supplementary_news.content: 越南湄公河三角洲地区E-Dengue早期预警系统用于主动登革热防控的经济学评价:一项研究方案 《PharmacoEconomics - Open》:Economic Evaluation of an E-Dengue Early Warning System for Proactive Dengue Prevention in the Mekong Delta Region, Vietnam: A Protocol 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月28日 来源:PharmacoEconomics - Open 2.0 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Protocol Open access 摘要 背景:已开发多种登革热早期预警工具,但少有成功整合至常规监测系统。E-Dengue工具依据“Useful, Usable, and Used”框架设计,旨在预测越南湄公河三角洲地区(MDR)提前3个月的登革热流行。该方案概述一种早期预警系统的经济学评价,其中E-Dengue预警触发主动登革热防控干预。 方法:将开展基于社会视角的经济学评价,并与整群随机对照试验(cRCT)并行。比较E-Dengue早期预警系统与常规实践的成本和结局。主要结局指标为伤残调整生命年(DALYs),次要结局指标为登革热病例数。通过疾病成本子研究(cost-of-illness substudy)量化登革热病例的平均成本,该子研究利用医院账单记录、对患者和非正式照护者的结构化调查以及文献证据综合。E-Dengue的成本效果将在2年时间范围内评估,分别表示为每避免1个DALY和每避免1例登革热病例的增量成本,并与预设成本效果阈值比较。采用单因素和概率敏感性分析(one-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses)评估结果稳健性。 讨论:证明E-Dengue具有成本效果,将为支持其整合至MDR常规监测提供严格证据,并可能支持其在越南其他地区和条件相似国家推广和适配。反之,若E-Dengue不具成本效果,该研究将为未来早期预警工具的设计和实施提供关键教训。 试验注册号:ACTRN12626000402347。 论文解读:原文为一项健康经济学评价方案,未报告实证结果。登革热(dengue)由Aedes蚊传播,在热带和亚热带国家负担高;气候变化、全球流动和城市化使全球发病率显著上升,东南亚在发病率、死亡率和伤残调整生命年(DALYs,disability-adjusted life years)上受影响最重。越南登革热年报告病例波动明显,2021—2025年报告数从69,140至345,234不等,且因无症状或轻症漏报,估计总病例为442,911—2,603,443,经济负担为US$29.77 million—US$94.87 million(2016价格);湄公河三角洲地区(MDR,Mekong Delta Region)发病率最高。现有媒介控制以化学、生物和/或环境管理为主,无单一措施优于其他,联合干预最有效但时间可持续性有限、需周期性重复;Wolbachia感染蚊释放和登革热疫苗仍需更多有效性、安全性和成本效果证据。早期预警系统(EWS)有潜力,但应用受模型准确性、数据及时性与质量、整合至国家监测系统以及将模型输出转化为行动的能力限制。E-Dengue依据“Useful, Usable, and Used”框架开发,利用流行病学和气候数据在区域卫生中心(RHC,Regional Health Center)水平提前3个月预测流行,并形成用户友好开源软件平台,目标整合入MDR常规监测;因公共资源有限,使用前需量化其价值。研究人员开展与平行组两臂cRCT并行的健康经济学评价,遵循健康经济评价报告规范(CHEERS 2022,Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standard 2022),比较E-Dengue预警触发主动干预与常规实践;主要结局为DALYs,次要结局为登革热病例,采用社会视角和2年时间范围,计算增量成本效果比(ICER,incremental cost-effectiveness ratio),并与预设支付意愿(WTP,willingness-to-pay)阈值比较。原文指出,若具成本效果,可支持整合、优化预算和人力资源并可能推广;若不具成本效果,可为未来EWS设计实施提供教训;若效力不足,可用经验成本数据在不同假设效力下建模;无论结果如何,均可为EWS和数字健康技术评估提供案例证据。 欢迎下载《重组激酶全方位解析:高效生产、严格质控与前沿应用》 领 取 关键技术方法(≤250字):在越南MDR的118个RHC开展两臂平行cRCT,干预臂由E-Dengue提前3个月预警触发主动物理灭源与教育、信息与沟通(EIC,education, information, and communication),非干预臂常规实践并平行开展幼虫调查;采用社会视角成本效果分析,疾病成本子研究在Dong Thap省Dong Thap医院和Cao Lanh综合医院招募135例门诊和135例住院患者及非正式照护者,结合医院账单、结构化问卷和文献综合;以看似无关回归(SUR,seemingly unrelated regression)估计增量成本与DALYs/病例,计算ICER,并行单因素和概率敏感性分析。 研究结果(方案设计):原文为方案,以下为方案规定的分析产出。研究现场:MDR覆盖>40,000 km2、人口17.43 million,行政改革后为五个半省、555 communes、128 RHCs,排除后118 RHCs入组,前Long An地区按地理属MDR纳入。研究设计:在2026和2027年两个登革热季节开展两臂平行cRCT,排除10个RHCs(8个避免污染、2个岛屿)后按59/59随机分配;两臂按越南卫生部指南常规防控,干预臂每月E-Dengue预警触发主动干预和幼虫调查,非干预臂仅幼虫调查;主动干预在预测流行月前1个月于高历史发病communes实施物理灭源(无杀虫剂)和全communes EIC,CDC于灭源前1天、后1天、后3周调查幼虫,非干预臂平行两次间隔4周。成本数据的样本量与抽样:主动活动成本在59个干预RHC、常规活动成本在118个RHC收集;疾病成本子研究在Dong Thap省两家医院作描述性单臂横断面调查,按Johnston et al.公式以V=0.15、Cv=0.75估算n≈97,补偿后目标135例住院和135例门诊及照护者。数据收集:健康结局指标中主要结局DALYs=YLD+YLL,采用0.0307和0.0351残疾权重并考虑33%患者后急性症状平均11.2个月;次要病例数来自常规监测,住院病例用1.2扩展因子校正,按非正式照护64.1%、门诊23.3%、住院12.6%估算;成本估计采用社会视角,以2024年世界银行平均汇率折算美元并用GDP平减指数或CCEMG–EPPI Cost Converter v1.7调整通胀;E-Dengue工具开发与运行成本来自项目、越南国家卫生与流行病学研究所(NIHE,National Institute of Hygiene and Epidemiology)等财务报告,设备基础设施按3%折现年化;主动干预成本来自项目/NIHE财务报告;常规登革热控制成本来自省疾病控制中心(CDC,Centers for Disease Control)、两臂收集,人力资源成本仅在Dong Thap省收集;疾病成本在两医院收集直接医疗、直接非医疗和生产力成本,直接医疗取2025年账单,直接非医疗和生产力由护士用结构化问卷访谈,非正式照护按US$17.32/例(2024价格)假设,生产力成本用人力资本和机会成本法。成本效果分析:EpiData/Excel录入、R分析,以RHC水平SUR估计增量成本和健康结局并调整基线协变量,计算ICER;成本不折现、YLL按3%折现、时间2年;基础WTP阈值0.5×人均GDP=US$2533(2025价格),敏感性用0.34×和1×人均GDP,病例结局WTP为每例估计成本;行单因素和概率敏感性(Monte Carlo,DALYs/成本用Gamma分布、病例用Poisson分布)分析,并报告成本效果平面、成本效果可接受性曲线及卫生服务视角分析。伦理批准:访谈前取得书面知情同意,方案获NIHE IRB–07/2023和University of Queensland 2023/HE001441批准。 讨论部分总结:该方案提供可推广至其他病媒传染病EWS的成本效果评价方法;据研究人员所知,这是首个估计任何EWS成本效果的研究,而现有EWS如D-MOSS、DART和EWARS的开发运行成本信息有限。原文指出三项局限:RHC和省工作人员常规防控成本仅在一个省收集,可能高估或低估;无法捕获全部常规防控成本,如志愿社区团队及整体传染病监测成本中归因登革热比例;患者成本来自单一省两家医院,单位成本可能不反映五个半省异质性,研究用单因素(均值±标准差或±25%)和概率敏感性分析处理。政策意义:评估有效性和成本效果对卫生部、CDC及省/commune利益相关者关键;若有效且具成本效果,可支持整合至MDR常规实践,首次引入主动成分以降低成本效果方式减少发病和局部暴发,并优化预算与人力,可能推广至越南其他地区和相似条件地区;若不具成本效果,提示不应常规使用,可能因高成本或缺乏效力;若缺乏效力,可用经验成本数据在不同假设效力下建模;若结果不确定,可进一步识别不确定性驱动因素并开展亚组分析。 研究结论(译文):无论cRCT和成本效果分析结果如何,所积累的证据将有助于政策制定者和实践者评估其他EWS或类似新技术的经济影响。该cRCT及成本效果分析将作为一个重要案例研究,提供与EWS和数字健康技术评估相关的重要证据和经验教训,而当前文献中此类证据仍相对有限。 Carlo,DALYs/成本用Gamma分布、病例用Poisson分布)分析,并报告成本效果平面、成本效果可接受性曲线及卫生服务视角分析。伦理批准:访谈前取得书面知情同意,方案获NIHE IRB–07/2023和University of Queensland 2023/HE001441批准。讨论部分总结:该方案提供可推广至其他病媒传染病EWS的成本效果评价方法;据研究人员所知,这是首个估计任何EWS成本效果的研究,而现有EWS如D-MOSS、DART和EWARS的开发运行成本信息有限。原文指出三项局限:RHC和省工作人员常规防控成本仅在一个省收集,可能高估或低估;无法捕获全部常规防控成本,如志愿社区团队及整体传染病监测成本中归因登革热比例;患者成本来自单一省两家医院,单位成本可能不反映五个半省异质性,研究用单因素(均值±标准差或±25%)和概率敏感性分析处理。政策意义:评估有效性和成本效果对卫生部、CDC及省/commune利益相关者关键;若有效且具成本效果,可支持整合至MDR常规实践,首次引入主动成分以降低成本效果方式减少发病和局部暴发,并优化预算与人力,可能推广至越南其他地区和相似条件地区;若不具成本效果,提示不应常规使用,可能因高成本或缺乏效力;若缺乏效力,可用经验成本数据在不同假设效力下建模;若结果不确定,可进一步识别不确定性驱动因素并开展亚组分析。研究结论(译文):无论cRCT和成本效果分析结果如何,所积累的证据将有助于政策制定者和实践者评估其他EWS或类似新技术的经济影响。该cRCT及成本效果分析将作为一个重要案例研究,提供与EWS和数字健康技术评估相关的重要证据和经验教训,而当前文献中此类证据仍相对有限。 supplementary_news.title: 登革热VS基孔肯雅热:症状对比、传播途径和预防措施
supplementary_news.excerpt: 所谓“蚊媒传染病”,就是蚊子在叮咬时把病毒或寄生虫“快递”到人体内的疾病;国内需要重点盯防的有登革热、基孔肯雅热、寨卡病毒病、乙型脑炎和疟疾等。 今天,我们先锁定由伊蚊“投递”的两大热门疾病——登革热与基孔肯雅热。 它是由登革病毒引起的,经伊蚊叮咬传播的虫媒传染病。据世界卫生组织统计,全球每年约有1-4亿人感染,其中美洲、东南亚和西太平洋区域发病最为严重,亚洲约占全球疾病负担的70%。

supplementary_news.excerpt: 近日,厦门海关所属海沧海关通过船方代理报告和登临检疫,在船员样本中检出1例登革病毒核酸阳性。厦门海关立即排查处置,并将相关信息通报地方卫生健康、疾控、边检及海事等部门。据地方卫生健康部门反馈,该船员已在医院进行后续治疗。 该文观点仅代表作者本人,搜狐号系信息发布平台,搜狐仅提供信息存储空间服务。
